prompt.context: Booz Allen was recently hired to work with the newly appointed VP of International Business at SunCo, a small-to-mid-sized CPG company with 95% of its sales in the US. SunCo has 3 product lines; the majority of its sales and the focus of this case are on its sun care products (e.g., sun tan lotion). SunCo was recently acquired by a large CPG conglomerate called ParentCo, which has a broad international presence mainly selling batteries and shaving-related products. ParentCo wants to double SunCo's international sales in the sun care product division by 2010. Currently SunCo's international sales are seemingly random with no real vision or strategy behind them, and distribution is spread across diverse markets.
prompt.question: If you were tasked with this project, how would you begin to approach solving the problem of doubling international sales for SunCo? (Note: ParentCo wants any growth to be self-funding — no large capital expenditures.)

clarifying_info.q: What is the current level of international sales that we need to double?
clarifying_info.a: The case does not give an exact current figure; focus on what it takes to double whatever the baseline is.

clarifying_info.q: What markets does SunCo currently operate in internationally?
clarifying_info.a: Distribution is in diverse markets. LATAM is the largest international market (30% share in Mexico, Chile, Argentina); SunCo is #1 in Australia; minimal presence in South Korea, China, India; 1% share in EU.
SunCo has 2 sun care brands with 60 SKUs each (120 total); they are #2 and #3 in the US market and together are larger than #1.

clarifying_info.q: What capabilities does ParentCo have internationally?
clarifying_info.a: ParentCo has well-established international distribution reaching even the most local levels such as corner grocery stores, and a sales force experienced in selling distinct product categories (batteries and shaving products).

framework: Markets & Customers: Assess overall market dynamics (size, growth, customer segments, geographies where ParentCo operates); understand customer demographics, needs, preferences, and current product/brand usage in each region
Competitors: Identify companies in each market, their market shares and growth rates, product differentiation and branding; overlay competitor share with each region
Company (SunCo + ParentCo): Assess SunCo's existing brands, SKUs, and current international share; assess what ParentCo adds (distribution reach, capital constraints, sales force, warehousing)

questions.prompt: Section 1 — Initial structure: How would you structure your approach to doubling SunCo's international sales?
questions.guidance: Candidate should use 3 C's (Customers/Markets, Competitors, Company) or an equivalent structured framework. Strong answers drill into sub-buckets: market size/growth/segments, competitor share/differentiation, company capabilities and ParentCo synergies. Candidate should note the self-funding constraint upfront.

questions.prompt: Section 2 — Market prioritization: Given the market data below, which region(s) should SunCo target? EU: $3B, 6% growth; APAC: $1B, 12% growth; LATAM: $1B, 12% growth. SunCo has 1% EU share; 30% share in Mexico/Chile/Argentina; #1 in Australia, sporadic elsewhere.
questions.guidance: Candidate should weigh market size (EU largest) vs. growth (APAC/LATAM highest) vs. existing footprint. Strong answer: LATAM is most attractive because growth is high (12%), customer preferences mirror the US (functional use), and SunCo already has 30% share in three anchor markets. APAC is high-growth but requires re-branding (beauty positioning) and lacks footprint. EU is large but SunCo has only 1% share and a brand/preference mismatch (customers prefer cosmetic brands like Loreal/Nivea). Candidate should proactively ask whether the LATAM anchor markets (Mexico/Chile/Argentina) already cover the required uplift — answer is they get partway but not fully, so additional LATAM expansion is needed. Brazil, Puerto Rico, Colombia are identified as priority expansion countries.

math.setup: LATAM anchor markets provide partial uplift; need to determine residual gap. No precise arithmetic is required but candidate can sanity-check: if current LATAM share = 30% of some subset, 12% annual market growth with steady share improves revenue but may not double total international sales alone.
steps: Acknowledge 12% market growth on 30% share in Mexico/Chile/Argentina generates incremental revenue
Note interviewer confirms this gets partway but not fully to the doubling target
Conclude that new country entries (Brazil, Puerto Rico, Colombia) in LATAM are needed to close the gap
math.answer: LATAM expansion (existing anchor markets + new entries: Brazil, Puerto Rico, Colombia) is the recommended priority.

questions.prompt: Section 3 — Go-to-market for Brazil: What would you consider in your go-to-market strategy for Brazil?
questions.guidance: Candidate should cover the 4 P's plus regulatory/tariff considerations. Strong answer covers: (1) Pricing — price relative to competition (cost-plus and WTP also valid frameworks); (2) Place/Distribution — identify which retail channels are used (beach shops, grocery stores, etc.), shelf placement, in-store displays; (3) Product — decide which brand(s) and how many of the 120 SKUs to launch, label changes to Portuguese; (4) Promotion — low-cost localized marketing (beach signage, point-of-sale) given the self-funding constraint; (5) Regulatory/Tax — government approval needed for chemically-based products, tariffs and tax structure that could erode margins.

questions.prompt: Section 4 — Distribution economics: SunCo currently sells a case of product to distributors for $100. Distributors mark up the case 45–50% to retailers (e.g., $150). What would be the benefit of taking distribution in-house using ParentCo's network?
questions.guidance: Strong answer should identify: (1) Cost savings from shared warehousing with ParentCo's existing inventory; (2) Sales force leverage — ParentCo's sales force already sells across distinct categories (batteries to shaving products) and can add sun care to the same customer set; (3) Billing and payments synergy — ParentCo handles these functions already; (4) Margin improvement — instead of paying a 45–50% distributor markup ($50 on a $100 case), SunCo could pass through a lower markup (30–40%) to retailers, stimulating demand while maintaining or improving operating margins. Candidate should also note the nuance: retailers are sophisticated and will likely demand a share of the cost savings rather than passing them on to end consumers.

math.setup: Distributor currently marks up $100 case by 45–50%, selling to retailers at ~$150 (a $50 markup). If ParentCo distribution replaces third-party distributor, the markup to retailers could be reduced.
steps: Current: SunCo sells at $100; distributor adds $50 markup (50%); retailer pays $150
In-house: SunCo leverages ParentCo infrastructure (shared warehouse, existing sales force, shared billing); incremental cost to SunCo is lower than $50
Potential retailer price: mark up only 30–40%, e.g., $130–$140 instead of $150
The $10–$20 savings per case can be used to lower retailer price (stimulating demand) or retained as margin
Caveat: retailers will likely negotiate to capture some of the savings themselves
math.answer: Taking distribution in-house via ParentCo can reduce the distributor markup from 45–50% to approximately 30–40%, improving economics for SunCo and/or stimulating retailer demand, while leveraging existing warehousing, sales force, and billing infrastructure at minimal incremental cost.

brainstorming.prompt: What are the key factors and risks to consider in expanding SunCo's sun care products into new LATAM markets (e.g., Brazil)?

categories.name: Market Attractiveness
ideas: Market size and growth rate (12% annually)
Customer preferences (functional use, similar to US)
Competitive landscape — top 5 players own 80% share in all markets

categories.name: Company Readiness
ideas: Existing brand equity and SKU portfolio (120 SKUs across 2 brands)
ParentCo distribution reach to local-level retailers
Sales force capability to add a new product category

categories.name: Go-to-Market Levers
ideas: Choice of which brand(s) and how many SKUs to launch first

categories.name: Risks & Barriers
ideas: Tariffs and tax structures eroding margins
Retailer negotiating power capturing distribution cost savings
Limited brand recognition in new markets
Need to avoid over-extension given self-funding constraint

recommendation: SunCo should prioritize LATAM expansion, leveraging its existing strong share in Mexico, Chile, and Argentina as a platform while entering Brazil, Puerto Rico, and Colombia as priority new markets
SunCo should route distribution through ParentCo's established international network to minimize capital investment and reduce distributor markups from 45–50% to 30–40%
risks: Retailers may capture the distribution cost savings rather than passing them through to consumers or SunCo margins
APAC and EU remain lower-priority but competitor entrenching could close the window over time
Over-extension across too many SKUs in new markets could strain limited resources under the self-funding constraint
Regulatory and tariff hurdles in Brazil could delay or erode economics of market entry
next_steps: Quantify the revenue contribution of Brazil, Puerto Rico, and Colombia required to bridge the gap to doubling international sales
Conduct detailed in-country assessment: regulatory requirements, tariff structure, preferred retail channels, and competitive pricing in Brazil
Work with ParentCo to define a distribution agreement and cost-sharing model for incremental sun care volumes
Determine launch assortment — likely a focused subset of SKUs from one brand in Portuguese packaging — rather than full 120-SKU rollout
